body_es: El rebase reescribe el historial de una rama tomando sus commits y reaplicándolos, uno por uno, sobre la punta actual de otra rama, en lugar de mezclar ambas historias con un commit de fusión. El resultado es una secuencia lineal: parece que el trabajo se hubiera hecho siempre encima de la última versión de la rama base, aunque en realidad Git generó commits nuevos con hashes distintos para cada commit original, porque el contenido del padre cambió. Esa reescritura es justamente el riesgo del rebase: si esos commits ya se compartieron con otras personas (por ejemplo, ya se hizo `push`), reescribirlos rompe el historial que otros ya descargaron y provoca conflictos difíciles de resolver en equipo. Por eso la regla práctica es usar rebase solo en ramas locales, antes de compartirlas. Por ejemplo, si `feature/new-api` tiene dos commits sobre una versión antigua de `master`, y mientras tanto `master` avanzó con un commit de corrección, `git rebase master` desde `feature/new-api` reaplica esos dos commits encima del nuevo `master`, produciendo hashes nuevos y un historial lineal en `git log --oneline`. Si aparece un conflicto durante el rebase, se resuelve el archivo, se hace `git add` y se continúa con `git rebase --continue`. Un error común es hacer rebase de una rama compartida y luego un `push --force`, sobrescribiendo el trabajo de otros sin avisar.
body_en: Rebasing rewrites a branch's history by taking its commits and reapplying them, one by one, on top of another branch's current tip, instead of merging both histories together with a merge commit. The result is a linear sequence: it looks as if the work had always been done on top of the base branch's latest version, even though Git actually generated new commits with different hashes for each original commit, because the parent's content changed. That rewriting is exactly the risk of rebasing: if those commits were already shared with other people (for example, already pushed), rewriting them breaks the history others already downloaded and causes conflicts that are hard to resolve as a team. That is why the practical rule is to use rebase only on local branches, before sharing them. For example, if `feature/new-api` has two commits on top of an older version of `master`, and meanwhile `master` advanced with a fix commit, `git rebase master` from `feature/new-api` reapplies those two commits on top of the new `master`, producing new hashes and a linear history in `git log --oneline`. If a conflict appears during the rebase, you resolve the file, run `git add`, and continue with `git rebase --continue`. A common mistake is rebasing a shared branch and then running `push --force`, overwriting other people's work without warning.
example_code:
master = [("a1b2c3d", "Add app.js entry point and .gitignore")]
feature = master + [("5b3c2d1", "Add login function"), ("f1e2d3c", "Add API endpoint")]
new_shas = ["7fa1b20", "7fa1b21"]

def rebase(branch, onto, new_shas):
    base_shas = {sha for sha, _ in onto}
    unique = [msg for sha, msg in branch if sha not in base_shas]
    replayed = list(zip(new_shas, unique))
    return onto + replayed

master.append(("9a8b7c6", "Fix typo in README"))
new_feature = rebase(feature, master, new_shas)
print("Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/new-api.")
for sha, msg in reversed(new_feature):
    print(f"{sha} {msg}")
